doc.title: Jon Hendricks — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Four Brothers and early New York
title: Lambert arranges Four Brothers for eight voices
summary: Lambert wrote the eight-voice arrangement in twenty minutes; vocal arrangements were taken from instrumentals, and the first release was split in two sides.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Was it arranged for just you and Dave, or were there other singers as well?

It was arranged for eight voices: four – let me see – six men and two women. Two of the men would be Dave and me. It was done so fast. I’m still amazed to this day. He just did it. Just wrote it out like you write a letter. He wrote that arrangement. It was amazing.
Was Dave responsible for a lot of the actual vocal arrangements in Lambert, Hendricks, and Ross?

The vocal arrangements were taken from the instrumentals. We just sang the instrumentals. We sang the instrumental arrangements. But he took the notes down, so that those of the singers who could read had notes to read. Of course the notes meant nothing to me.

I just heard it. He had that Four Brothers thing ready in about 20 minutes, as I say. We began work then. George Handy was right in with us. He was in with the whole thing. He just couldn’t believe it. He says, “This is incredible.” They both were saying things like, “I never saw anything like this.” It was a new thing. It was the ideas of Eddie Jefferson and Eddie Jefferson taken into the orchestral form.

Extended, yeah. So we did it first for this guy Teacho Wilshire, and he came up with the idea that since it was such a fast song, we should do side 1 and side 2 and slow it down. I didn’t necessarily agree with this, but at that time I wasn’t prone to speak out. I thought the people that made these kinds of decisions knew everything. Do you have a question?
